title: Central Warehouse (1927–2026/27), 143 Montgomery St
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: The 11-story refrigerated warehouse was built by the New York Central in 1927. Final demolition began September 21–22, 2026, starting with its rail bridge, and is expected to run through the winter. It will leave a cleared 1.1-acre lot beside I-787.

notes.Look for: the teardown itself; watch from public streets, since Amtrak tracks run alongside.
notes.Hook: the last days of Albany's biggest eyesore, on its 99th birthday.

title: Empire State Plaza footprint: the lost South End blocks
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: In 1962 the state took 98.5 acres by eminent domain and razed roughly 40 blocks, displacing thousands of residents. Hudson Avenue lost its blocks between South Swan and Eagle; Cathedral Academy and a former executive mansion at Hawk and Lancaster went too.

notes.Look for: stub ends of Hudson Ave and Lancaster St at the Plaza's edges, and the Mansion District just south, the part that survived. The County Hall of Records has "Then and Now" street guides and 1930 ward maps for overlays.

links: Albany County Hall of Records exhibit

title: Old State Capitol (1809–1883) and Capitol Hill's vanished state buildings
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: Philip Hooker's capitol stood on the north side of State Street, just east of Eagle, in front of today's Capitol. Lafayette was received there in 1824 and Lincoln lay in state there in 1865; it was razed in 1883. The adjoining State Library, the Old State Hall at Lodge and State (gone by the late 1930s) and Congress Hall hotel are all gone.

notes.Look for: the 1886 bronze tablet marking the old main entrance on the East Capitol Park lawn.

title: Fort Frederick (1676–1789), Gallows Hill and the fort burial ground
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: The fort sat in the middle of State Street just west of Lodge, opposite St. Peter's Church, rebuilt in stone between 1702 and 1735. Its stones went into street widening and church buildings. The 1886 tablet adds "Gallows Hill to the South, Fort Burial Ground to the North."

notes.Look for: three markers, including one at the base of the clock in the State Street median at Eagle.
notes.Hook: a fort under four lanes of traffic.

title: Fort Orange site, foot of State Street
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: The Dutch West India Company fort of 1624 stood southeast of the State Street marker, by the river. Archaeologists excavated it around 1970–71 before the I-787 ramps closed over it; it is listed on the National Register as an archaeological site.

notes.Look for: the state marker on the plaza at Broadway and State; the ramps near the Dunn Memorial Bridge sit on the site.

title: Albany Basin, the Pier and Erie Canal Lock 1
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: From 1825 a long pier enclosed the riverfront, creating a basin for about 1,000 canal boats and 50 steamboats; a weigh lock stood just north. The basin was filled for I-787 and the Corning Preserve. The original Lock 1 was rediscovered in 2002 in an industrial lot in North Albany.

notes.Look for: the Urban Cultural Park marker downtown, and old cut stone along Erie Boulevard, which follows the canal bed.

links: Empire State Plaza: Erie Canal in Albany

title: Maiden Lane Bridge, the "South Bridge" (1871–c.1969)
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: A rail swing bridge crossed from the foot of Maiden Lane to East Albany, with extra spans over the Basin and past the Albany Yacht Club's island. It came out after the New York Central moved passenger service to Rensselaer in 1968.

notes.Look for: the alignment at about 42.6478, -73.7458; check the river walls for any surviving pier stubs.

title: Harmanus Bleecker Hall (1889–1940), Washington Ave at Lark
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: Opened October 9, 1889 with 1,985 seats, the largest theater in the Capital District. It became Proctor's Harmanus movie house around 1929 and burned in May 1940. The main Albany Public Library now stands on the site.

notes.Hook: the region's biggest stage is under the library.

title: Tweddle Hall and the Ten Eyck Hotel, State and North Pearl
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: Tweddle Hall was Albany's leading concert hall for decades. It came down around 1912 to enlarge the Ten Eyck Hotel, which was itself razed around 1970 for a bank. Two layers of lost buildings on one corner, at about 42.6499, -73.7528.

title: Wellington Hotel Annex
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: The annex behind State Street's Wellington Row was imploded on August 23, 2014; the historic façades on State Street were kept. Good for a façade-versus-loss segment.

title: Delavan House hotel site, Broadway at Steuben
sec: Albany: downtown, waterfront and the Empire State Plaza footprint
story: A big railroad-era hotel that burned in 1894. Union Station rose on the site around 1900; the station closed in 1968 and is now Kiernan Plaza. Dates not confirmed against the Albany Institute photo files.

title: Washington Park: the State Street Burying Ground
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: From about 1800 the city's main cemetery covered much of today's park. Burials were moved to Albany Rural Cemetery in the 1860s (a city list of removed graves was printed in 1866) and the park was rebuilt over it around 1870. Local historians think some remains were left behind; a Lutheran ground also sat on the State Street side at Willett.

notes.Look for: the lawns between Knox and Robin streets, State St to Hudson Ave. City archaeological monitoring still applies to digging here.

links: NYS Museum: burial in early Albany

title: Albany Almshouse and its potter's field, New Scotland Avenue
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The county almshouse ran here from 1826 to 1926, with a pauper cemetery. A 2002 dig for a medical research building expected about 200 graves and found roughly 1,200; they were studied by the State Museum and reburied at Albany Rural. The almshouse stood behind the WWI-era armory, diagonally across from Albany Med.

title: Dudley Observatory's two lost buildings
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The first observatory (1856) stood on "Goat Hill," now Dudley Heights in Arbor Hill, until railroad vibration ruined its readings. The second (1893) rose on the almshouse grounds on South Lake Avenue, was sold to Albany Med in 1963, burned in 1970, and gave way to the Capital District Psychiatric Center.
links: Hoxsie: Mrs. Dudley builds an observatory

title: Albany Penitentiary (1848–1931), Myrtle Ave and Lark St
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: A 12-acre prison bounded by Myrtle Ave, Lark St, Leonard Place and South Knox St. It closed in 1931 and was razed in 1933, when wreckers found isolation "dungeons." The Stratton VA Medical Center now covers the site; its mugshot ledgers are at the County Hall of Records on Tivoli Street.

title: Mona Terrace caskets, off Delaware Avenue
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: On September 29, 2009, road crews hit five wooden caskets. Officials suspected a Roman Catholic cemetery that had been moved around 1910, apparently not completely. Neighbors already knew of an "old burial ground" nearby.

title: The three lost kills: Beaver, Rutten and Foxen
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: Albany grew around three creeks, all now piped underground. The Rutten Kill's ravine was filled under the Empire State Plaza; its only open stretch is dammed as Washington Park Lake. The Beaver Kill still carves the Lincoln Park ravine, and an 1886 tablet at South Pearl and Arch marks where it was "arched over."

notes.Look for: the wooded ravine below Lincoln Park, with old brick shafts and grates.

title: Sheridan Hollow and the Foxenkill
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The Foxenkill was put in a culvert around 1840 and the ravine filled for workers' housing. Residents used outhouses and wells into the 1920s; Dinah Jackson, Albany's first known Black property owner, held lots here, and Tories were reputedly hanged and buried in the hollow. Digs for a state parking garage produced a State Museum exhibit.

title: Van Rensselaer Manor House site, North Broadway
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: North Albany and the Lumber District
story: The patroons' 1765 manor house stood just off Broadway near Loudonville Road, beside the mouth of Patroon Creek. Hemmed in by railroads, it was dismantled in 1893; Marcus T. Reynolds rebuilt much of it as a fraternity house at Williams College, which tore it down in 1973. A hall from it is at the Metropolitan Museum.

notes.Look for: the Tivoli, Manor and Thacher street area near the Nipper building. A 1946 writer said the exact spot was already hard to find.

title: Albany Lumber District
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: North Albany and the Lumber District
story: From North Ferry Street north about 1.5 miles, between the Erie Canal and the river, slips and lumber piles made Albany the country's top lumber market by value in the 1870s. The Irish neighborhood here was nicknamed "Limerick." Erie Boulevard follows the canal bed; I-787 covers the slips.

notes.Look for: old cut stone blocks along Erie Blvd.

title: Beverwyck Brewery site, North Ferry and North Lawrence
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: North Albany and the Lumber District
story: Quinn & Nolan's brewery (Nolan was Albany's first Irish Catholic mayor) became Beverwyck, then Schaefer, which closed it in 1972. The 1870s building resisted demolition charges in 1976 and had to come down brick by brick.

title: Rathbone & Sard building fire, July 2024
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: North Albany and the Lumber District
story: A preservation group reported that a building tied to the Rathbone & Sard stove works, dating to the 1830s near the old canal north of downtown, burned on July 13, 2024 and was quickly demolished. Confirm the address in news archives; it is a brand-new empty lot from the stove era.

title: West Albany Shops (1854–1964)
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The New York Central bought 250 acres here in 1854 and grew it to about 350. At the turn of the century over 6,000 people built and repaired locomotives and cars. Car shops closed in 1954, the site sold in 1955 and most buildings came down in 1964; stockyards and slaughterhouses lingered longer.

notes.Look for: the main line still in use; railfans say one shop building survives, so check before you go.

title: First steam train junction, Madison Ave and South Allen St
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The Mohawk & Hudson's 1831 line began here, where it met the Great Western Turnpike, and ran 16 straight miles to Schenectady. Inclined planes were added at both ends; in 1844 the line moved north to Tivoli Hollow, abandoning this end.

notes.Look for: the 2021 Pomeroy marker, then trace the 1831 alignment on 1830s–50s maps.

title: Albany's lost breweries
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: Only Beverwyck, Hedrick and Dobler survived Prohibition. Dobler (founded 1865) closed in 1960 and its main building was razed that year, but its horse carriage house still stands. Jacob Kirchner's brewery sites at 9 Central Ave and 8–10 Sherman St are reported as vacant lots.

title: Bleecker Reservoir, now Bleecker Stadium
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: The city's 1850s reservoir sat inside 18-foot earth berms. It was retired in 1932 and turned into a stadium in 1933–34 as a New Deal project; the berms are why it feels like a bowl. Stadium and Swinburne Park joined the National Register in 2018.

title: Six Mile Waterworks and the four-mile brick conduit
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: Engineer William J. McAlpine dammed Patroon Creek in 1851–52 to make 40-acre Rensselaer Lake, Albany's only supply until 1875. An egg-shaped brick conduit, about four miles long and four million bricks, carried water to Bleecker Reservoir. The lake served until 1926 and became a park in 1956.

notes.Hook: follow a buried 1850s aqueduct across the city.

title: Tivoli Lakes and Tivoli Hollow
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
story: In 1851 the city dammed lower Patroon Creek into Upper and Lower Tivoli Lakes. The reservoir was obsolete by the early 1900s and became a dump before its rebirth as an 82-acre preserve. The 1851 dam survives, and 1,500 feet of the creek were daylighted in 2019.

title: Kenwood: the Rathbone villa and Sacred Heart convent
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: Estates, islands and the south edge
story: Joel Rathbone built his Kenwood estate on 1,200 acres; the Society of the Sacred Heart bought it in 1859. After Doane Stuart left in 2009 it sat empty, and on March 23, 2023 fire destroyed the main building, which was then demolished. The sisters' cemetery was not sold.

notes.Look for: the cleared site off Mt. Hope Drive and Route 9W, the cemetery, and a cobblestone smokehouse. Private property.

title: Mount Hope: the Prentice estate
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: Estates, islands and the south edge
story: Ezra Prentice's hilltop estate overlooked the South End. The mansion and family vault are gone; the Ezra Prentice Homes on South Pearl, at the foot of the hill, carry the name. Old atlases will show the drive and grounds.

title: Westerlo Island: Curtiss's runway and Quentin Roosevelt Field
sec: Albany: neighborhoods, buried creeks, cemeteries, water works and the city edge
sub: Estates, islands and the south edge
story: Glenn Curtiss took off from here on May 29, 1910 for the first Albany–New York City flight. The island became Albany's municipal airfield, named for Quentin Roosevelt in 1919, until the county airport opened in 1928. Once five islands, it was joined to land in the 1930s and opened as the Port of Albany in 1932.

notes.Lead: the first Quentin Roosevelt field was a former polo ground in Loudonville.

title: "The Hill" paupers' cemetery, near the county airport
story: About 12 acres between the county hockey rink, the jail, the airport, the Ann Lee Home and Shaker Ridge Country Club. The county buried the unclaimed here from 1926 to about 1946, possibly up to 1,500 people, with no known map. A crumbling brick building on top is believed to have held caskets through the winter.

title: Hawkins Stadium and Mid-City Park, Broadway, Menands
story: The Albany Senators played here at Chadwick Park, then at Hawkins Stadium from 1928 to 1959, drawing over 210,000 fans in 1948. The park was sold for back taxes and razed in 1960. The Mid-City Shopping Center, built about 1960, covers both the stadium and the old Mid-City amusement park.

notes.Hook: stand at home plate in a parking lot.

title: Schuyler Flatts burial ground
story: In 2005 a sewer crew just north of Albany uncovered the remains of 14 people, almost certainly enslaved Africans on the Schuyler farm. After study at the State Museum they were reburied at St. Agnes Cemetery on June 18, 2016. The farm site is now Schuyler Flatts Cultural Park; the old Schuyler house is long gone.

title: Karner (Center Station): the Pine Bush town that never happened
story: A Mohawk & Hudson stop from 1831, halfway between the two cities. George Karner platted streets and lots that mostly never sold; only Thompson Street was built. Nabokov later named the Karner blue butterfly from specimens here. Walkers can find the station, schoolhouse and ice house sites along a remnant of Center House Road.
links: Save the Pine Bush walk notes

title: Crescent Station and the Troy & Schenectady Railroad grade
story: The Troy-owned railroad opened in 1842; service between Crescent Station and Green Island ended in 1976. Its bed is now the Mohawk-Hudson Hike/Bike Trail, so look for culverts, cuts and station sites along it.

title: Albany Glassworks site, Guilderland hamlet (Hamilton)
story: Begun around 1785 on the Hungerkill near today's Route 20, it made bottles and window glass, about 500,000 feet a year by 1813. Alexander Hamilton and Philip Schuyler had money in it, and the company village was named Hamilton. It folded in 1815; a 2-acre archaeological site is on the National Register.

notes.Look for: two markers near Route 20; later a hat factory and foundry used the site.

title: Voorheesville Army Depot, Guilderland Center
story: A sprawling WWII Army supply depot, later renamed the Voorheesville Holding and Reconsignment Point. It is now the Northeastern Industrial Park off Route 146 and County Route 201; part is still a federal stockpile site.

notes.Look for: depot-era warehouses, rail spurs and "Depot Road," now School Road.

title: Knox Cave: a dead show cave
story: Roaches' Cave was opened commercially in 1933 by D.C. Robinson as Knox Cave, drawing up to 1,000 people on weekends, with a dance and skating venue outside. A couple married in its Big Room in 1958; tours ended around 1958–61 after Robinson died. A rusting steam shovel once stood by the entrance.

notes.Access: Northeastern Cave Conservancy preserve; permit required, closed October 1 to mid-May for bats. Marker on Route 156 north of Town Hall Road.

title: Thacher Park's CCC traces
story: A Civilian Conservation Corps camp at Thompson's Lake cut trails and did forestry; a later camp at Thacher built the first section of the stone overlook wall on the escarpment. An old train wheel used as a CCC fire gong survives in the area.
links: NYS Parks: history of Thacher Park

title: Indian Fields: the hamlet under Alcove Reservoir
story: Albany dammed Hannacroix Creek in 1928–32 and flooded the hamlet of Indian Fields. Fourteen small burying grounds were cleared; workers probed with iron rods for remains, and many reburials went unmarked in the new Indian Fields Cemetery on Route 143. Next door, Alcove's 1892 mill fire left a lone chimney, now on the National Register.

title: Coeymans Landing: brickyards, ice houses and a lost "castle"
story: Powell & Minnock, the last brickmaker in New York, ran from the late 1880s to 2001; its sheds were razed and the Port of Coeymans sits on the site. Ruins of a Knickerbocker Ice Company house stand north of the landing. The first house, "Coeymans Castle," stood at Westerlo and First streets until 1833.

notes.Look for: brickyard worker housing and bottle dumps.

title: Van Wies Point, Glenmont
story: William Welch kept the Van Wie's Point light from about 1858 until he died in 1910 at 93, the longest-serving keeper on the Hudson. A state marker notes the Van Wie dock, leased in 1835 to the Hudson River Steamboat Co. as an Albany terminal. What survives of the light station is not confirmed.

title: One Monument Square: the City Hall pit
sub: Downtown holes and lost civic buildings
story: Troy's 1974 City Hall on River Street was torn down in 2011, leaving a 1.2–1.5 acre waterfront hole. Four or more redevelopment plans have collapsed since. In February 2026 the mayor vowed to build, and in July the council moved to transfer the site to the Troy Local Development Corporation for a $50 million project.

notes.Hook: 15 years as Troy's biggest empty lot; check whether work has started.

title: The 1876 City Hall on the old burial ground, Third and State
sub: Downtown holes and lost civic buildings
story: Troy chose the old Third Street Burial Ground, donated land once held by the Vanderheydens, for its Victorian City Hall. It burned in a spectacular 1938 fire that also toppled the First Baptist spire next door. Barker Park and St. Anthony of Padua now occupy the site.

notes.Hook: a city hall on a cemetery, now a pocket park.

links: Hoxsie: Yes, there was a City Hall

title: Troy Union Station (c.1903–1958)
sub: Downtown holes and lost civic buildings
story: A Beaux-Arts station by Reed & Stem filled the block east of Union Street, from Broadway to Fulton. At its peak it handled over 130 passenger trains a day for five railroads. It closed and was demolished in 1958; the site became parking.

notes.Look for: the track alignment through the block. Only CSX's Troy industrial track still enters the city.

title: The Great Fire of 1862 footprint
sub: Downtown holes and lost civic buildings
story: Sparks from the wooden railroad bridge to Green Island started the May 10, 1862 fire that gutted central Troy. Lost: the Union House, Washington Hall and Fulton House hotels, Troy City Bank, Warren's Female Charity School and two factories. Gurley rebuilt its instrument works at once; that 1862 building still stands.
links: Hoxsie: Troy before and after the fire

title: Troy's lost theaters
sub: Downtown holes and lost civic buildings
story: The 3rd Street lot at No. 12 burned twice (Adelphi 1862, Griswold Hall 1871) before the Griswold Opera House rose in 1871; it was razed in 1951 for a Woolworth's, itself razed for the Uncle Sam Atrium. The Troy Theatre (323 River St) fell in 1973 and rerouted River Street runs over it. The Lincoln (73 3rd St) is a parking lot.

notes.Look for: Rand's Opera House, later the "Hall-Rand" bowling hall, at Congress and Third.

title: Burden Upper Works and the water wheel pit
story: Henry Burden's 1851 wheel, 62 feet across and 22 feet wide with 36 buckets, was the most powerful vertical water wheel ever built and a likely inspiration for the Ferris wheel. Abandoned in the 1890s, it lost a support pier in 1914 and was hauled off as scrap. The 50-acre works is a National Register archaeological site.

notes.Look for: a brick conduit with iron bands at the end of the upper raceway, the wheel mural at Mill, Water and High streets and Burden Ave, and Burden Pond Preserve's 43 acres of trails above.

title: America's first Bessemer steel plant and the Monitor's armor
story: Winslow, Griswold & Holley started an experimental Bessemer plant in Troy on February 16, 1865, the first in the U.S. Troy's Rensselaer and Albany iron works had already rolled the USS Monitor's armor plates and rivets. The riverfront became Troy Steel & Iron, then a 1924 coke plant, and is now a state remediation site off Water Street.

notes.Access: fenced brownfield; view from Burden Ave and the river trail.

title: The stove works: Fuller & Warren's Clinton Foundry
story: Albany and Troy were America's stove capitals, with 349 recorded makers over 130 years. Fuller & Warren's big riverfront works stood between Madison and Monroe streets just below the Poestenkill and is gone. By contrast, the 1846 Empire Stove Works at Second and Ida streets survives as a restaurant.

notes.Lead: the Troy Co-operative Foundry site (1866–1891), River St and Glen Ave in Batestown.

title: Poestenkill Gorge mill ruins
story: A 37-acre National Register district of mill ruins from the 1600s to the mid-1900s, below falls that drop about 175 feet in five steps. Mills here included Griswold Wire Works, Tompkins Brothers machine works and Manning Paper. Look for a mill foundation with one standing brick arch, bricks stamped "Bleau," and old bridge rods.

notes.Access: Poestenkill Gorge Park off Linden Ave; stay off the cliffs, which have caused deaths. Tiny Mount Ida Cemetery, with some of Troy's oldest stones, is nearby.

title: Prospect Park: the Warren estate and the dead Bintz pool
story: Troy bought the Warren family's Mount Ida estate for $110,000 and opened it in 1902, designed by Garnet Douglass Baltimore, RPI's first Black graduate. The Warren mansion (a military museum) and Vail House ("the Casino") are gone. Its 1926 above-ground Bintz pool closed in 1994 and sits abandoned.

notes.Lead: the estate's "Gingerbread" gatehouse was moved to College Ave around 1904 and later demolished.

title: Mount Olympus, North Troy
conf: Verified (history); Lead (how much was cut away)
story: A rocky bluff on the old road to Lansingburgh, crowned by a "Round House" that burned on the night of February 13, 1830. Geologists collected fossils here in the 1840s. USGS still marks a summit near the river; compare with 1850s maps to see what streets and rail lines removed.

title: Rensselaer Park, Lansingburgh
story: A private pleasure ground from 1867 with a trotting track and a skating pond, where local militia staged a mock Monitor-versus-Merrimac battle in the 1870s. The Union baseball club played here in 1868, around 108th–110th streets and 8th–9th avenues. It later became an amusement park with a Figure 8 coaster; Knickerbocker Park took over the site in 1924.

title: Troy & New England trolley, Albia to Averill Park (1895–1925)
story: A nine-mile electric line ran from Troy's Albia neighborhood up the Wynantskill valley to the Sand Lake resorts. A 2024 marker at the Arlington Hotel (once the Elkhorn) notes it was Stop 22. Trace the grade, stops and resort sites along Route 66 and the Wynantskill.

title: Clinton's Ditch under the Harmony Mills
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: When the original 1825 canal was rerouted around 1841, its bed became power canals for the mills. Original Locks 37 and 38 now serve as foundations for Harmony Mills buildings, visible through periscope viewers at the Clinton's Ditch Interpretive Plaza on North Mohawk Street. Remnants of Lock 39 sit at the south end of the same park.

notes.Hook: look through a periscope at an 1825 lock under a factory.

title: The ten double locks of the Enlarged Erie (Locks 9–18)
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Cohoes held the canal's densest flight: ten double limestone locks, each lifting about 10 feet. Lock 10 was dismantled in the 1950s; Lock 11 survives behind a church, and 12, 16, 17 and 18 still show cut stone, towpath and prism. Lock 16 is behind Harmony Mill No. 1, near Vliet and Harmony streets.

title: The Cohoes Mastodon pit, Harmony Mill No. 3
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Digging foundations for Mill No. 3, nicknamed the "Mastodon Mill," uncovered a mastodon skeleton in a glacial pothole in 1866. It now stands in the State Museum. Pair a museum shot with the mill exterior and the old "Juncta" site, the 1823 junction of the Erie and Champlain canals.

title: Matton Shipyard ruins, Van Schaick Island
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: John E. Matton moved his yard here in 1916 and built barges, tugs and police boats until 1983. The state bought it in 1989; roofs fell and floods took buildings until it was listed on the National Register in 2009. The 1921 canal motorship Day Peckinpaugh is berthed here.

notes.Access: part of Peebles Island State Park; ask Parks about access to the yard itself.

title: Union Bridge piers: the first bridge over the Hudson (1804–1909)
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Theodore Burr's 726-foot timber bridge to Lansingburgh went up in seven months in 1804, was roofed in 1814 and burned on July 10, 1909. The original stone piers are encased inside the concrete piers of today's Troy–Waterford Bridge; the toll sign and a timber model are at the Waterford Museum. Two later Cohoes–Lansingburgh bridges also burned, the last on March 4, 1920.

title: Waterford's 1841 fire lots
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: The village's municipal parking lot covers the sites of two 19th-century hotels destroyed in the 1841 fire, with no known images of either. Town Hall replaced an 1873 building that burned in 1914. Use the village walking-tour brochure as a map.

title: "The Crossroads": the old side-cut locks at Lock 2 Park
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Enlargement-era side-cut locks from about 1860 linked the canals to the Hudson here. Today they act as a spillway when Barge Canal Lock 2 operates; drained in winter, the old chambers show their stonework.

title: Ford's Green Island plant (1923–1988)
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: After camping here in 1919 with Edison, Firestone and Burroughs, Henry Ford built a hydro-powered plant that made radiators and heater cores, employing close to 1,000. It closed in 1988 and the factory was torn down in 2004; the hydroelectric station still runs. The four friends' carved initials became the plant cornerstone.

notes.Also here: River Park marks where the 1823 State Dam crossed to Troy.

title: Watervliet's buried side-cut locks and the canal through the Arsenal
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Troy merchants paid for an "upper side cut" at today's 23rd Street (1823) so boats could skip the Albany Basin; a lower side cut ran just south of the Arsenal. The lock remains were photographed in 1970 and reportedly filled in to preserve them. Photos show the abandoned canal through the Arsenal at 13th Street.

notes.Look for: the 1850 West Troy Weighlock building, which survives in Maplewood Historic Park, Colonie.

title: Al-Tro Park, the island amusement park
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: Named for Albany and Troy, it sat on an island cut off by the Hudson and the Erie Canal, reached by trolley or steamboat. A fire that started in an ice cream booth swept it on September 14, 1913. A new marker stands in Menands.

title: East Albany's riverfront freight yards
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: On July 5, 1861 fire destroyed the Albany & Boston Railroad's freight depots in East Albany, now Rensselaer, along with loaded canal boats; losses topped half a million dollars. The later New York Central yards here were mostly cleared for redevelopment. Compare 1880s Sanborn sheets with the riverfront today.

title: Albany & Hudson third-rail trolley (1899–1929)
sec: Cohoes, Waterford, Green Island, Watervliet, Menands and Rensselaer
story: An electric line ran from Albany through Rensselaer and Columbia counties to Hudson, with a resort stop at Electric Park on Kinderhook Lake. A 1901 crash outside Greenbush killed at least seven. Its 36-mile bed is now the Albany–Hudson Electric Trail (AHET), so station sites and culverts are on a public trail.

title: The African American burial ground: Veeder Avenue to Vale
story: Schenectady's Black community buried its dead on Hamilton Hill along Veeder Avenue until the ground was moved to Vale Cemetery beginning in 1863, with no surviving records. Ground-penetrating radar in July 2026 found 300 to 400 unmarked graves in Section F and an intact headstone from about 1829 buried just under the turf. The old Veeder Avenue ground was sold off for development.

notes.Look for: Section F at Vale, then walk Veeder Ave for the original site.

title: The Stockade's lost churchyard, Green and Front streets
story: The First Reformed Church's burying ground near Green and Front streets was overgrown and "unsanitary" by the 1850s and was moved to Vale between 1859 and 1879. Pair it with the Vale story above: two whole cemeteries relocated within a generation.

title: Queen's Fort, Front, Ferry and Green streets
story: After the 1690 massacre, a triple-stockade fort went up here around 1705, rebuilt in 1735 on a 10-foot stone wall: 100 feet square, with 20-foot blockhouses at the corners and six cannon. It was dismantled after the Revolution. The "Lawrence the Indian" statue marks its northeast blockhouse; the earlier Corlaer's Fort (1661–1690) stood a few hundred feet west.

title: Burr's Mohawk bridge abutment, foot of Washington Avenue
story: Theodore Burr's 997-foot wooden suspension bridge to Scotia opened in 1808; in 1857 its floor gave way under about 50 cattle. An iron bridge reused its piers from 1874, later carried trolleys, and served until 1926. Its abutment is still visible where Washington Avenue meets the river, aimed straight at Scotia's own Washington Avenue.
links: Hoxsie: the bridge that preceded it

title: Erie Boulevard: the canal filled with coal ash
story: Schenectady's stretch of the canal closed in 1917 and was filled largely with furnace ash; Erie Boulevard opened with a 1924 Progress Exposition and was finished by 1926. Liberty Street had to be lowered after its canal bridge came out, and old Dock Street became the sidewalk. A grain elevator once stood at Pine and Jefferson; the first Proctor's theater, later the Erie, opened onto the towpath.

notes.Look for: the 2025 bicentennial plaque on Erie Blvd and the unusual width of the street.

title: Union Station (1908–1971), Erie Blvd and Liberty St
story: The Beaux-Arts station closed in 1969. Penn Central sold it to the city for $20,000 in December 1970 and it was demolished in 1971 for a parking lot. A plain 1979 Amtrak station on the site was itself razed in 2017; the 2018 station borrows the old design.

title: ALCO's 1,000-foot shops, now Mohawk Harbor
story: Locomotives were built here from 1848 to January 1969. Building 62 (later GE's Building 332), finished in 1905 and nearly 1,000 feet long, carried "AMERICAN LOCOMOTIVE" in brick; Building 70 ran about 930 feet. Both fell in 2014 for Mohawk Harbor and Rivers Casino.

notes.Look for: ALCO Heritage Trail signs along the river.
notes.Lead: some ALCO-era buildings may survive east of Maxon Road and North Jay Street.

title: "Engine Hill": the Mohawk & Hudson's western end, Crane Street
story: The 1831 railroad's western terminal stood on Crane Street, long called Engine Hill; a 1938 city marker sits at Crane and 3rd Ave (about 801 Crane St). A stationary engine hauled cars down the incline toward the city until the line was rerouted in the early 1840s.

title: Downtown's lost theaters and corners
story: John Eberson's atmospheric Plaza Theatre (617 State St) opened August 28, 1931 with about 2,400 seats and was razed in 1964; the lot sat empty for decades. The State Theater at State and Erie was leveled in the late 1970s for parking, as were the Ellis and Bucci buildings on that corner. The Strand (409–411 State) is gone too.

notes.Background: a fire in 1819 destroyed 169 buildings, which is why downtown dates from after that year.

title: Brandywine Park, the city's trolley park
story: The Schenectady Railway opened Brandywine Park in 1896 at the city's then-edge. The city grew around it, and the company sold the grounds to St. Luke's Church in the early 1920s. Use 1900s maps to place the picnic grove and pavilions.

title: Rexford Aqueduct ruins
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
sub: Bridges and aqueducts over the Mohawk
story: The 1825 Upper Mohawk aqueduct was replaced in 1841–42 by a 1,160-foot stone aqueduct on 14 piers. Most of it came down around 1916–18 for the Barge Canal. Two arches survive on the Niskayuna bank and one on the Rexford bank; you can stand on them, and a county marker went up in 2025.

notes.Also here: old Erie Lock 21, used as a boat launch by the Schenectady Yacht Club, and remains of Lock 22.

title: The "longest trolley bridge in the world" piers, Aqueduct–Alplaus
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
sub: Bridges and aqueducts over the Mohawk
story: Just upstream of the Route 146 bridge, the Schenectady Railway's 1,800-foot steel trestle stood on limestone piers. The center piers were removed for the barge channel; piers still line the south side, with three on each bank. North of the river the right-of-way survives as an embankment trail at Bruce Road in Alplaus.

notes.Look for: the Glenridge Road "trolley tunnels" farther north.

title: Crescent Aqueduct abutments
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
sub: Bridges and aqueducts over the Mohawk
story: The Lower Mohawk aqueduct carried the canal across the river at Crescent; the 1842 version was the longest aqueduct in the state. It was dismantled around 1914 for the Barge Canal, leaving only cut-stone abutment fragments on both banks.

title: Luna Park / Rexford Park (1901–1933)
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: Reached by a nickel trolley ride over the long bridge above, Rexford's park had a coaster, carousel and an early aerial swing ride. Wreckers began tearing it down on April 3, 1935, after a couple of years as a picnic grove. Concrete footings from the coaster and park buildings still sit in overgrown woods, according to Saratoga Today and the Clifton Park town historian; the bridge piers are the easy establishing shot.

title: Forest Park, Ballston Lake (1904–1927)
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: The GE-owned Schenectady Railway built a 144-acre park at the south end of Ballston Lake with a beach, ball fields and bike tracks. The company sold the land to campers in 1927 and trolleys stopped in 1940. The Ballston Veterans Bike Path follows the trolley bed past the site.

title: Enlarged Double Lock 23, Rotterdam
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: Built in 1841, it was the canal's busiest lock, passing about 47,000 vessels a season around 1880; one chamber was enlarged to take two boats lashed together. It sits overgrown beside the Mohawk-Hudson trail at Rice and Schermerhorn roads, about 3,000 feet from Barge Canal Lock 8.

title: Plotter Kill aqueduct arches, Rotterdam
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: Stone arches that carried the canal over the Plotter Kill, known in canal days as Van Slyck's or the Flat Stone Creek aqueduct. A small, little-visited ruin near the trail.

title: Schenectady Army Depot, Rotterdam (1918–1960s)
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: Built in 1918, it supplied 55 CCC camps in the 1930s, then grew to about 4,000 workers shipping vehicles in WWII. From 1948 to 1949 it processed the war dead returning home. The Galesi Group bought it in 1969 and it is now Rotterdam Corporate Park; a former Army housing area where Jimmy Carter once lived has a marker.

title: Scotia Naval Supply Depot, Glenville (1942–1971)
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: A 310-acre Navy depot near Thruway Exit 26 that employed over 2,000 people supplying the Atlantic fleet. Buildings were razed around 2012 and the federal government took on soil cleanup. Look for surviving rail spurs and warehouse slabs in the business park that replaced it.

title: Schoharie Crossing and the lost Fort Hunter
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: The 1841 Schoharie Aqueduct had 14 arches; 9 remain, and the site keeps the only two surviving locks of the original 1825 canal. Fort Hunter (1712) and Queen Anne's Chapel stood at the Mohawk village of Tiononderoge; the canal destroyed the chapel in the 1820s. Queen Anne's Parsonage is the fort's only surviving building.
links: HMDB: the fort by the village

title: Amsterdam's vanished Main Street
sec: Schenectady County and the lower Mohawk Valley
story: Urban renewal from the 1960s to the 1980s razed about 400 buildings and dropped a mall across East Main Street, cutting downtown in two. Route 5 now curves over the site of St. Mary's Institute near East Main and Schuyler Street. Good "drive through what was there" material with 1950s photos.

title: R. & W. Scott ice house ruins, Nutten Hook (Stuyvesant)
story: Built in 1885 with four elevators hauling ice from the river, it was the largest ice house on the Hudson. It later grew mushrooms and burned in 1934. A tall brick powerhouse and foundations remain on a 0.4-mile DEC loop at the end of Ice House Road, off Route 9J.

notes.Also here: the Newton Hook–Coxsackie ferry ran from 1820 to 1938, and the 1902–03 Cary brickyard left building ruins just south on 9J.

title: Empire Brickyard and the lost company town, Stockport
story: Jerome Walsh's yard between Gays Point and Little Nutten Hook grew a settlement called Walshville, renamed Empire, with a post office and reportedly 700 families. It closed before 1940 when the clay ran out. Six permanent kiln walls with firing arches survive, possibly the only such kiln remnants outside an intact Hudson Valley brickyard, plus bulkhead and rail-spur piers.

notes.Access: DEC's Charles Flood Wildlife Management Area.

title: Kingston's brickyards: Hutton, Staples and Shultz
story: Hutton ran from 1865 to 1980; its three steel kiln sheds, moved from Haverstraw in 1940, and a Lidgerwood crane survive as an event venue beside the Empire State Trail. Upriver at Malden, the Staples yard closed in 1958 and its gantry was removed around 2004–05; worker-house ruins remain. At East Kingston, the Shultz yard's brick flue still stands.

title: Coxsackie Light, Rattlesnake Island
story: A light stood on the north tip of the island from 1830; the last brick tower and keeper's house went up in 1868. It was razed in 1940. Look for the stone crib and riprap that protected the station, at about 42°22.5′ N, 73°47.4′ W.

title: Stuyvesant and Four Mile Point lights
story: The Stuyvesant light was deactivated in 1933 and destroyed. Four Mile Point, halfway between Athens and Coxsackie, had a keeper's dwelling called "old and beyond repair" in 1881. Of about 14 lighthouses once on the Hudson, only 7 or 8 stand.

title: Hudson–Athens Lighthouse (1874), at risk now
story: One of the survivors, but its wooden pilings are rotting and the building is shifting. It made the National Trust's endangered list in 2024, and in February 2026 the Trust reported damage worse than expected. Film it while it stands; tours run from Hudson.

title: Hudson: Diamond Street, Chapel Street and the General Worth
sub: River cities that cleared their own pasts
story: Diamond Street, now Columbia Street, was the state's most notorious red-light district until troopers raided it in June 1950; the worst of it, "The Block," ran between Third and Fourth streets, and many of its lots are now empty. Urban renewal erased Chapel Street in 1974 for Bliss Towers and demolished the 1837 General Worth Hotel, a National Register property.

title: Kingston: the Lost Rondout
sub: River cities that cleared their own pasts
story: In the 1960s federal urban renewal razed nearly 500 buildings on the Rondout's east side and displaced thousands, many of them Black families. The Cornell Steamboat Company's 1881 office was torn down in 1966; T.R. Gallo Park is on the site. The west side, including West Strand Row, survived.

notes.Source material: Gene Dauner's slides, used in the film "Lost Rondout."

title: Catskill village: the Prospect Park Hotel
sub: River cities that cleared their own pasts
story: A large hotel overlooked the Hudson at Catskill Point; a 1915 county history says it burned in 1914, and an 1851 fire had already taken the Irving House and two churches downtown. The site and dates are not confirmed with the Greene County Historical Society.

title: Hotel Kaaterskill site, South Mountain (1881–1924)
sub: The escarpment: three hotels and an incline (North-South Lake)
story: George Harding built it after the Catskill Mountain House refused his daughter's special diet; it was billed as the world's largest mountain hotel, and President Arthur stayed a week in 1884. A kitchen fire on September 8, 1924 burned it overnight, visible for miles. A low stone foundation, rusted metal and broken china remain in the woods on state land.

notes.Look for: the stone laundry/sawmill house near Scribner's mill on the loop back from the site.

title: Catskill Mountain House site (1824–1963)
sub: The escarpment: three hotels and an incline (North-South Lake)
story: America's most fashionable resort closed in 1942 and decayed until the state Conservation Department burned it at 6 a.m. on January 25, 1963. Only gateposts and the view remain, a short walk from North Lake on the Escarpment Trail.

title: Laurel House site, top of Kaaterskill Falls (1852–1967)
sub: The escarpment: three hotels and an incline (North-South Lake)
story: Peter Schutt's boarding house grew to hold about 300 guests at half the big hotels' prices; it even dammed Spruce Creek so the falls could be turned up for guests. The state bought it and burned it on March 1, 1967. Parts of the stone foundation sit by the creek above the falls, off Laurel House Road.

notes.Also here: the 1.5-mile Kaaterskill Rail Trail on the old railroad from Haines Falls station to Laurel House Road.

title: Otis Elevating Railway grade (1892–1918)
sub: The escarpment: three hotels and an incline (North-South Lake)
story: A cable funicular lifted cars of 75 to 100 passengers about 1,600 feet up the escarpment in roughly 10 minutes, from Otis Junction near Palenville to the Mountain House. It closed in 1918 and was sold for scrap; its coaches went to Chattanooga's Lookout Mountain incline. The scar is still visible, with a section of concrete trestle in the woods.

notes.Access: steep and unmaintained from below; hikers start near Boggart Road north of Palenville.

title: Grand Hotel, Highmount (1881–1966)
story: Built by the Ulster & Delaware Railroad on Monka Hill, its 418 rooms looked down the Big Indian valley to Slide Mountain. It closed in 1966 and later burned. Original stone walls, paths and the grand front staircase survive on the property at 111 Club House Drive; the railroad's Grand Hotel station and turntable site sit below.

title: Tremper House, Phoenicia (1879–1908)
story: Jacob Tremper's railroad resort on the slopes of Mount Tremper was dedicated by Henry Ward Beecher, and Oscar Wilde lectured there in 1882. After a fight over using it for tuberculosis patients, it sat empty and burned in 1908. Look for the terrace and drive on the hillside above the Esopus.

title: Overlook Mountain House ruins, Woodstock
story: The first hotel (1871) burned in 1875; its successor hosted the secret 1921 founding of the Communist Party of America and burned on October 31, 1923. Morris Newgold's concrete replacement was never finished and went to the state in 1940. Well known, but the communist-meeting angle rarely makes videos.

title: Grossinger's, Liberty (southern Catskills)
story: The Borscht Belt's best-known resort ran from the 1910s to 1986. Its last building came down on October 19, 2018, and a remaining structure burned in 2022. A true empty-lot story.

title: Dibble's Quarry, Platte Clove / Elka Park
story: A bluestone quarry worked until the late 1800s, said to have supplied New York City sidewalks. Anonymous builders stacked the waste slabs into thrones, chairs, tables and a firepit facing a huge valley view.

title: The tannery towns: Edwardsville, Prattsville, Palenville, Samsonville
story: About 64 tanneries stripped some 70 million hemlocks in the Catskills. Greene County had 56 in 1840 and just 9 by 1855. Col. William Edwards founded Edwardsville (now Hunter) in 1817; Zadock Pratt's Prattsville works employed about 2,000 from 1825 to 1845 before he moved on to Samsonville in Ulster County.

notes.Look for: old tan-bark roads in the Forest Preserve, Edwards's "Colonel's Chair" on Hunter Mountain, and Snyder's 1850 tannery site at Shandaken.

title: Gilboa under the Schoharie Reservoir (1920s)
story: New York City condemned the village, which had three churches, two hotels, a theater and its own electric plant. Crews burned about 430 buildings up to six miles upstream; on October 18, 1925 a fire took 18 downtown buildings while tourists watched from the hills. In droughts, traces of the old village reappear above the waterline.

notes.Look for: two Pomeroy markers, "Echoes of Gilboa" (numbered stones for unknown remains moved in 1921) and "New Gilboa" (2026).

title: The Ashokan hamlets (1907–1915)
story: About 2,000 to 2,300 people were moved, more than 500 buildings moved or razed, and some 2,600 graves from 32 cemeteries reburied. Eleven hamlets were flooded or relocated: Ashton, Boiceville, Brodhead's Bridge, Brown's Station, Glenford, Olive, Olive Bridge, Olive City, Shokan, West Hurley and West Shokan. Brown's Station and Olive City are under water.

notes.Look for: brown "Former site of" signs along Routes 28 and 28A.

title: The Sacandaga Valley (1930)
story: The Conklingville Dam's gates closed on March 27, 1930. All or part of ten communities went under: Batchellerville, Fish House, Osborne Bridge, The Vly, Cranberry Creek, Sacandaga Park, Day, Conklingville, Munsonville and Benedict, plus the tannery hamlet of Parkville. Crews moved 3,872 graves, removed four covered bridges and a rail bridge, dragged houses on skids, and burned what was left.

notes.Look for: markers at Batchellerville, Parkville and Conklingville.

title: French's Hollow under the Watervliet Reservoir, Guilderland (1915–17)
story: Typhoid-plagued Watervliet dammed the Normanskill in rural Guilderland. The mill hamlet of French's Hollow, whose first mill dated to 1795, was mostly destroyed, and the 1760 Wemple farmhouse near Fuller's Station was razed in 1915.

title: Indian Fields under Alcove Reservoir (1928–32)
story: See the Albany County section: Albany's water supply drowned this Coeymans hamlet and its 14 burying grounds.

title: Beyond your range: the 1950s Delaware reservoirs
story: Later NYC reservoirs drowned more villages: Pepacton (Arena, Pepacton, Shavertown, Union Grove), Cannonsville (Cannonsville, Rock Rift, Beerston) and Neversink.

title: Grand Union Hotel site, Broadway
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: It began as Gideon Putnam's 1802 boarding house and grew into the world's largest hotel, with a dining hall over 200 feet long. It was demolished in 1952–53 and replaced by a Woolworth's plaza. Its giant Adolphe Yvon mural, "The Genius of America," survived and hangs in Chancellor's Hall in the State Education Building in Albany.

notes.Hook: see the plaza, then the mural an hour south.

title: United States Hotel site, Broadway at Division Street
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: The first United States Hotel opened in 1824 and burned in 1865; its grander replacement was finished in 1874. Demolition ran from May 1945 to March 1946, and the corner sat nearly empty for years with a small concrete-block bar. Today shops, including one at 385 Broadway, stand on the footprint.

title: Congress Hall, under Congress Park
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: Gideon Putnam died in 1812 while building this hotel at Broadway and Spring Street; it was rebuilt in 1867–68. After years in decline, the village bought it with the Congress Spring bottling works and pavilions and razed them in 1911–13, erasing a stretch of Putnam Street. The northwest corner of the park, around the Spirit of Life memorial, covers the site.

title: Hotel Balmoral and its railroad, Mount McGregor
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: Joseph Drexel's narrow-gauge line climbed 10.5 miles from Saratoga in 1882, and in 1883 it tested Leo Daft's electric locomotive, the Ampère. His Hotel Balmoral opened beside the cottage where Ulysses S. Grant died in 1885; it burned in December 1897 and the railroad was dismantled soon after. The site sat inside a sanatorium, then a state prison, until 4 acres including the hotel site went to Grant Cottage in 2022.

title: Sans Souci Hotel block, Ballston Spa
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: Built by Nicholas Low in 1803, the Sans Souci was then the largest hotel in the country and filled the block bounded by Front Street, Milton Avenue, Washington Street and Spring Street. It later housed a law school and a ladies' seminary and was torn down in the winter of 1887–88. Down the street, the Eagle Hotel burned on July 8, 1932; the post office stands on its site.

title: Kaydeross Park, Saratoga Lake (1900–1987)
sec: Saratoga Springs, Ballston Spa and Mount McGregor
story: A trolley park reached by streetcar until 1925, it ran as an amusement park until August 1987, when its 40 acres were sold for 349 luxury housing units. Its 1910 carousel now spins in Congress Park, and Kaydeross Park Road is about the only other trace.

title: Courtland Street burial ground and "Repose of the Fallen"
story: On February 7, 2019 a crew digging a basement a block off Canada Street cut into an unmarked cemetery. State Museum researchers identified at least 44 people, patients of the 1776 Continental Army smallpox hospital at Fort George, where an estimated thousand died that year. They were reburied in Lake George Battlefield Park at the "Repose of the Fallen" memorial, dedicated in 2026.

notes.Hook: walk from the house lot on Courtland Street to the new memorial.

title: Prospect Mountain Cable Incline (1895–1903)
story: Built in six months for $120,000, it opened June 15, 1895 and hauled cars about 6,600 feet up to the Prospect Mountain House, almost 2,000 feet above the lake. It failed financially and stopped in 1903. The summit keeps its giant bull wheel and cable gears, masonry and interpretive signs; the hiking trail from the village follows the incline's route.

title: The first Fort William Henry Hotel (1855–1909)
story: The hotel at the head of the lake opened in June 1855 and grew to hold over 900 guests before burning on June 24, 1909. The D&H built a smaller replacement in 1911, which was itself razed in 1969; today's hotel (2004) imitates the 1911 building. Stoddard's photographs make great then-and-now material.

title: Graphite, the pencil boomtown (Hague)
story: Dixon's American Graphite Company mined Graphite Mountain from the 1880s until 1921, supplying Dixon-Ticonderoga pencils. The hamlet of about 400 had saloons, stores and a post office; when the mine closed, buildings were moved away. The mines now shelter about 125,000 hibernating bats of six species, and mill foundations remain in the woods.

notes.Access: mines are sealed for bats; much land is private. The Hague Historical Museum covers it.

title: Griffin ghost town (Wells, Hamilton County)
story: A tannery town built around Stephen Griffin II's 1880 tannery, later the Rice Emery Company's; it was sold in 1896 and the land went to the state. Griffin turned briefly to tourism and was finished by the 1930s. The tannery foundation with its pipes, small barn remains and the Girard House survive at the start of the Auger Flats trail.

notes.Lead: Wells residents reportedly hauled Griffin's foundation stones home.

title: Sacandaga Park, the amusement park under the lake
story: The FJ&G Railroad turned picnic grounds near Northville into a resort; after an 1898 fire it added a midway with a roller coaster, two carousels and a ballfield on Sport Island. Rising reservoir water in 1929–30 drowned the midway and the rail line. Its railroad station survives at 136 McKinley Ave and is on the National Register; stone pillars mark the old auto entrance.

title: Hammondville, the iron company town (Crown Point)
story: The Crown Point Iron Company's town peaked near 1,000 people, connected by a 13-mile narrow-gauge railroad to Lake Champlain, with ore shipped to Troy. It was abandoned in the 1890s when the venture failed. Crown Point iron also plated the USS Monitor, tying it to the Troy entry above.

notes.Access: mine shafts and private land; start at the Penfield Homestead Museum in Ironville and Monitor Bay Park's furnace site.

title: Adirondac (Tahawus) and the McIntyre furnace
story: The best-known ghost town in the state, built around an iron mine and reachable from a trailhead lot.
